001_moby_dick_opening.intro: Five devices in three lines, in reading order.

steps.note: 'Call me Ishmael. Some years ago…' — two statements, no connecting word. The reader supplies the connection, and trusts it, because they made it themselves.
The dashes — 'never mind how long precisely' — interrupt the sentence to hold back a fact. The holding back is the point: this is a man for whom the years blurred.
'Little or no money,' 'nothing particular' — saying it in negatives softens it. The narrator admits he is broke and aimless while sounding amused about both.
The opening has no connecting words at all; then the ands pile up: 'and nothing particular… and see…' The sentence drifts, and the conjunctions alone carry the drift.
'The watery part of the world' comes last, in the position English stresses most. The sea lands hardest because it arrives at the end.

001_moby_dick_opening.coda: Command, hedge, evasion, drift, horizon — five gestures in forty-five words, none stated, all performed.

003_tale_two_cities_opening.intro: Ten clauses, one famous comma splice.

steps.note: 'It was the' — ten times. When the frame never changes, all attention goes to the one word that does.

Each pair holds opposites in the same grammar: best against worst, hope against despair. The balance treats both as equally true. The sentence refuses to choose — and that refusal is the novel's argument.
Every clause has the same shape and nearly the same length: 'it was the ___ of ___.' The matching beat makes the opposites toll like a bell instead of just alternating.
Everything and its opposite, true at the same time. The sentence doesn't describe what revolutionary times feel like; it makes you feel it.
Ten full sentences joined by commas — normally an error. The splice keeps you from stopping: a full stop would let you rest, and rest would let you pick a side.

003_tale_two_cities_opening.coda: One pattern, repeated far past the usual limit, carrying a historical argument. The pattern never escalates; the effect on the reader does.

005_hamlet_to_be.intro: The most famous unfinished sentence in English. It never completes its own question — and that is the portrait.

steps.note: 'To be, or not to be' — no subject. No one is doing the being. Hamlet weighs existence without ever attaching it to himself.
To suffer against to take arms — passive against active, in matched frames. But the halves aren't equal: quiet dignity on one side, doomed grandeur on the other.
'The slings and arrows of outrageous fortune' — suffering pictured as weapons fire. Slings and arrows are aimed. In this picture, fortune isn't indifferent; it's hostile.
'Take arms against a sea of troubles.' You can't fight water with a sword — and that's the point. The impossible image shows the plan is impossible.
'Whether 'tis nobler…' opens a question the rest of the sentence should answer. The answer never comes. The sentence can't decide; neither can he.

005_hamlet_to_be.coda: Syntax is character: what the mind cannot do, its grammar cannot do.

026_declaration_independence.intro: One sentence built to make a debatable claim sound like arithmetic.

steps.note: 'We hold' — not 'we believe,' which can be argued with, and not 'we assert,' which sounds like effort. To hold a truth is to have it already. And 'we' quietly includes every reader.
'Self-evident' skips the entire argument. A truth that needs no proof gets none — and the reader, credited with finding it obvious, doesn't ask for any.

'That all men… that they are endowed… that among these are.' Three claims hang from one verb, joined by one repeated word. They read like clauses of a single contract — hard to deny one without denying all.
'Life, Liberty and the pursuit of Happiness' climbs: from staying alive, to being free, to — note the wording — not happiness itself but the chase. The last item is carefully not promised.

'Are created… are endowed' — passive voice, but with the actor named: 'by their Creator.' That keeps men as the subject and puts their rights at the point of stress. Compare 'mistakes were made,' where the passive hides the actor instead.

026_declaration_independence.coda: The style is not decoration on the argument. It is the argument.

027_gettysburg_address.intro: The opening sentence does half the speech's work: consecrate the ground, refound the nation.

steps.note: 'Four score and seven' instead of 'eighty-seven.' The old-fashioned counting makes the number sound ancient and scriptural. A battlefield is not consecrated in the language of an invoice.
The rhythm copies Genesis and the Psalms. His listeners all knew one book; the sentence borrows that book's authority without naming it.
The nation is 'conceived' and 'brought forth' — born, with Liberty as the condition. What is born can die, and can be born again. The figure sets up the speech's ending.

'Conceived in Liberty, and dedicated to the proposition' — two matched verb forms: how the nation began, and what it promised. When Lincoln later asks for 'a new birth of freedom,' he is collecting on this pair.
'All men are created equal' — Jefferson's words, exact and uncredited. Quoting them here turns the Declaration into a 'proposition': something still to be proven, on this field.

027_gettysburg_address.coda: No ornament, no side trips. Every device moves the same direction: from the nation's birth to its test.

028_i_have_dream.intro: The most famous anaphora in American English — and the frame is the least of it.

steps.note: 'I have a dream' — present tense, first person. The dream exists now, in one particular man, as a fact no vote can undo.
The phrase returns, and each return raises the stakes: the nation, then the states, then his own children. Same words, higher price each time.
'This nation will rise up' — will, not may. He states the future as fact until the audience starts to believe it.
He quotes Jefferson in full, standing at Lincoln's memorial. The country's founding sentence, read back to it like an unpaid IOU.
The colon sets the creed out like evidence in court. The dream is only that the country keep its own written word.

028_i_have_dream.coda: Old devices, new aim: every figure points the nation's own words back at it.

082_one_art.intro: A poem about losing everything, told like instructions for a card trick. The gap between the tone and the subject is the poem.

steps.note: 'The art of losing' — losing, a thing that happens to you, is renamed as an art, a thing you practice. The grammar claims a control the speaker doesn't have.
'Isn't hard to master,' 'no disaster' — each denial names the very word, hard or disaster, that the speaker is trying not to believe.
The poem says teaching; it means grief. Reader and speaker both know 'isn't hard to master' is false. We watch a lie practiced with perfect technique.
Things are 'filled with the intent to be lost.' If the keys meant to go, nobody lost them. The blame moves from the speaker to the objects.
'Their loss is no disaster' sounds like a verdict. Then four stanzas test it against bigger and bigger losses until it breaks. It was never a conclusion — it was a hope.

082_one_art.coda: No tears anywhere in it — just grammar arranged to keep the speaker standing. That is what understatement is for.

090_blood_meridian.intro: Two sentences: three words, then forty. The ratio is the style.

steps.note: 'They rode on.' Done. Then the second sentence pours out with no transition — the flat statement first, the flood after.
'They rode… They rode' — the smallest repetition there is, returning through the whole novel like hoofbeats. It never builds; it persists, like weather.
'Antique and diffuse and the wholes thereof' — and, and, and. Nothing ranked above anything else. The sentence keeps going because the ands won't let it stop.
'The wholes thereof' — Bible English. The old wording gives a band of killers the sound of prophecy, and the desert the feel of the Old Testament.
After all that grandeur: 'scattered like paper in the wind.' Not chaff, not stars — paper. The great purpose ends up compared to litter.

090_blood_meridian.coda: Three beats, then forty. The prose is scored like music.
